reason: The text demonstrates that Yahweh's primary concern is the liberation and welfare of the entire Hebrew people from slavery, not merely the leaders. Throughout the passage, Yahweh repeatedly sends Moses and Aaron with the message 'Let my people go' (שַׁלַּח אֶת־ עַמִּי). When the people suffer increased burdens and their officers appeal to Pharaoh, Yahweh responds by sending plagues specifically to secure the people's freedom. When Moses himself complains about the suffering brought upon the people, Yahweh assures him of divine action to deliver the entire nation. The narrative structure shows that while leaders (both Hebrew and Egyptian) experience difficulty, Yahweh's empathy is directed toward the collective people facing oppression. The plagues are not punishing the leaders preferentially—rather, they pressure Pharaoh to release all the enslaved Hebrews. The statement's claim of empathy only toward leaders while lacking empathy for the people contradicts the text's consistent emphasis on liberation for the whole community.
